title: Cap. IV open: Arminianorum sententia — from Pontiffs to interpolators; Arminius on faith foresight
pass_a_gloss: Chapter IV. The Arminians' sentence is set forth, and their arguments are refuted. The Pontiffs' arguments having been omitted and rejected, we must next deal with those who have interpolated this controversy, certain vocabularies and forms of speaking having been changed, yet the foundations of the errors themselves having been retained. Among these Jacobus Arminius holds the chief place, a learned man and of sharp genius, but who assigned little to the judgment of the ancient Church, nothing to the Reformed. He therefore, lest he seem too crude in constituting his defense, was unwilling to maintain that any man is predestinated from foreseen works or merits (as some speak) but from foreseen faith; he was unwilling also to assert of this faith what they boldly affirmed of works, that it is the cause of our predestination to glory: but with softened words he teaches that it is only a condition, or something decently antecedent.
pass_b_english: Cap. IV. The Arminians' position is set out and their arguments refuted. Pontiff arguments omitted and rejected, we next deal with those who interpolated this controversy — changing some words and phrases while keeping the same error foundations. Chief among them is Jacobus Arminius: learned, sharp-minded, yet little regard for the ancient Church's judgment and none for the Reformed. Lest his defense look too crude, he would not hold anyone predestinated from foreseen works or merits (as some say) but from foreseen faith; nor would he boldly call that faith the cause of our predestination to glory as they did of works — with softened words he calls it only a condition, or something decently antecedent.
source_text: Cap. IV. Arminianorum sententia exponitur, atque argumenta refelluntur. Omissis atque rejectis Pontificiorum argumentis, cum iis deinceps agendum est, qui interpolarunt hanc controversiam, mutatis quibusdam vocabulis, et loquendi formulis, ipsa tamen errorum fundamenta retinuerunt. In his principem locum obtinet Jacobus Arminius, vir doctus et acri ingenio, sed qui parum tribuebat antiquae Ecclesiae judicio, nihil Reformatae. Is igitur, ne crassus nimis videretur in constituenda sua defensione, noluit tueri ullum hominem praedestinari ex praevisis operibus aut meritis (ut loquuntur quidam) sed ex fide praevisa; noluit etiam quod illi de operibus audacter afferebant, de hac fide asserere, illam esse causam praedestinationis nostrae ad gloriam: sed vocabulis emollitis, docet esse tantum conditionem, aut quiddam decenter antecedaneum.
